title: Maths Online Practice Tests & Quizzes for Grade 2 (A Weekly Plan + Free Quiz)
meta_title: Maths Online Practice Tests for Grade 2 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: How online maths quizzes help Class 2 kids with instant feedback, which topics to test, a simple weekly plan, plus a free 8-question quiz to try.
excerpt: A short online quiz can do something a worksheet cannot: tell a seven-year-old the instant they slip, before the mistake sets in. Here is how to use Grade 2 maths quizzes well — and how not to — plus a free one to try today.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Watch a Class 2 child do a page of subtraction and you will often see the same borrowing mistake repeated fifteen times before anyone notices. The worksheet gets marked that evening, or the next day, and by then the wrong method is already a habit. A short online maths quiz flips that: it tells the child — and you — the moment something slips. That single feature, instant feedback, is why maths online practice tests and quizzes for Grade 2 have become such a useful tool for parents at home, especially in busy households where nobody has time to mark by hand.

But an online quiz is a tool, not a tutor. Used well it sharpens; used badly it turns maths into a screen-time argument. Here is how I would use them with a seven-year-old, what to test, and a weekly plan that keeps the total screen time under half an hour.

Why a quiz beats a worksheet for feedback

The maths itself is identical — 47 + 26 is the same sum on paper or on a screen. What changes is the feedback loop. Three things make a good online quiz genuinely helpful at this age:

  • Instant marking. The child sees a tick or a cross straight away, while the sum is still fresh, so the correction actually lands.
  • Low pressure. There is no red pen and no teacher waiting. A child will happily retry a question they got wrong on a screen, whereas a crossed-out sum on paper can sting.
  • Built-in spaced practice. Because a quiz takes five minutes, you can come back to the same topic on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. That spacing — returning to a skill just as it starts to fade — is what moves a fact from ‘got it today’ to ‘knows it for good’.

One honest caveat before we go further. A quiz shows you whether a child got the answer, not always how they got there. For a skill like subtraction with borrowing, I still want to see the working on paper now and then. Use the quiz to catch the slip; use a worksheet to see the method.

Which Grade 2 topics are worth testing

Not every topic suits a quick multiple-choice quiz. The ones that do are the fact-and-procedure skills a child should eventually answer without stopping to think. In my experience these are the highest-value Class 2 topics to drill online:

TopicWhy quiz itExample question
Place value (hundreds, tens, ones)Underpins every later sumThe 4 in 347 stands for how many?
Addition with regroupingSpeed and accuracy matter38 + 27 = ?
Subtraction with borrowingThe most common error spot52 − 17 = ?
Times tables (2, 5, 10)Pure recall — ideal for quizzing5 × 6 = ?
Money (₹ rupees and paise)Real-life, motivating₹20 − ₹13 = ?
Telling time (to the half hour)Reading, not calculatingHalf past 3 is written as?

Topics I would not lean on quizzes for: word problems that need a child to explain their reasoning, and anything visual like symmetry or 2D shape properties, where drawing beats picking an option. Save those for paper.

How to use quizzes well — and not overdo the screen

The biggest risk is turning a five-minute tool into a forty-minute one. A Class 2 child does not need a maths app open for an hour; that is how you get glazed eyes and guessed answers. My rule of thumb is one short quiz a sitting, and never more than one or two sittings a day.

Keep the child in the driver’s seat

Sit next to them, not across the room. When a cross comes up, resist the urge to say the answer. Ask ‘how did you work that out?’ and let them talk it through — that one question does more for understanding than three more quizzes. Reading the explanation together after a wrong answer is where the real learning happens.

Watch for guessing

If a child is clicking options in under two seconds, they are guessing, not thinking. Pause, cover the screen, and ask them to say the answer out loud first. A quiz only helps if the child is actually doing the maths.

A simple weekly quiz plan for Grade 2

Ten to fifteen minutes of maths a day, spread across the week, beats a long weekend cram every time. Here is a light structure that has worked for parents I know, built around short quizzes with paper backup twice a week:

  • Monday: place value quiz (5 minutes), then talk through anything missed.
  • Tuesday: addition with regrouping — quiz, then three sums on paper to check the method.
  • Wednesday: times tables of 2, 5 and 10 — a quick recall quiz.
  • Thursday: subtraction with borrowing — quiz plus paper working.
  • Friday: a mixed quiz covering the whole week, so the child has to choose the right method rather than being told which one.

That Friday mixed quiz is the important one. Practising one skill at a time is easy; deciding which skill a question needs is the real test, and it is where you will see whether the week stuck. Keep weekends free, or use them for a single money or time quiz tied to something real — totting up the change from a ₹100 note at the shop counts as maths.

The eight questions below cover exactly the Class 2 skills worth quizzing — place value, regrouping, borrowing, tables, money and time. Let your child try it, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.intro: Eight quick questions covering place value, regrouping, borrowing, times tables, money and time. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 2 maths within 100, tables of 2, 5 and 10, money and time

questions.q: In the number 347, the digit 4 stands for how many?
questions.explanation: In 347 the 4 is in the tens place, so it stands for 4 tens, which is 40.
8 + 7 = 15, so write 5 and carry 1 ten. 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 tens. The answer is 65.
You cannot take 7 from 2, so borrow a ten: 12 − 7 = 5, and 4 − 1 = 3. The answer is 35.
Five sixes make 30. Count in fives six times: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30.

questions.q: A pen costs ₹13. You pay with a ₹20 note. How much change do you get?
How do we write half past 3?
questions.explanation: Half past means 30 minutes after the hour, so half past 3 is 3:30.
The numbers go up in hundreds, so after 300 comes 400.
To multiply by 10, put a zero after the number: 6 becomes 60.

faq.q: Are online quizzes good for Grade 2 maths?
faq.a: Yes, for fact-and-procedure skills like tables, regrouping and place value, because the instant feedback catches a mistake before it becomes a habit. For word problems and reasoning, though, paper working is still better so you can see how the child thinks.

faq.q: How much time should a Class 2 child spend on maths quizzes a day?
faq.a: About ten to fifteen focused minutes, in one or two short sittings. A single five-minute quiz followed by a quick chat about any wrong answers does far more than a long session that ends in guessing.

faq.q: How do I stop my child just guessing the answers?
faq.a: Sit with them and ask them to say the answer out loud before they click. If they are choosing options in under two seconds, cover the screen and have them work it out first. A quiz only helps when the child is actually doing the maths.

faq.q: Which Grade 2 topics work best as quizzes?
faq.a: Place value, addition with regrouping, subtraction with borrowing, the 2, 5 and 10 times tables, money and telling time. Skip quizzes for symmetry, shapes and multi-step word problems — those are better on paper.
